tell: Great: taller, with a long kinked neck and a gape line that runs past the eye. Intermediate: smaller, shorter neck, and the gape stops below the eye.
Little: slim, with a black bill and yellow feet, and dashes about in the shallows. Intermediate: yellow bill and dark feet, and hunts slowly.
Little: much smaller, with a black bill and yellow feet. Great: far taller, with a long kinked neck and dark feet.
Cattle: small, stocky and short-necked, often with stock or on mown grass. Intermediate: taller and slimmer, and wades in swamps.
Royal: black spoon bill and black legs. Yellow-billed: pale yellow bill and legs, and prefers fresh water.
White Ibis: white body with a bare black head. Straw-necked: glossy dark back and wings, with straw-like plumes on the neck.
White-faced: blue-grey with just the face white. White-necked: bigger and darker, with the whole head and neck white.
Male Chestnut Teal is easy: green head, chestnut body. Females are harder: Grey Teal is paler with a whiter throat, Chestnut is darker overall.
Pacific Black Duck: bigger, with bold dark stripes across a pale face. Grey Teal: smaller and plain-faced, with a pale throat and red eye.
Plumed: pale tan, with long cream plumes along the flanks. Wandering: richer chestnut, with a dark cap and short flank plumes.
Australasian: tiny and dumpy, with a chestnut neck stripe when breeding. Great Crested: much bigger and long-necked, with a black crest and chestnut ruff.
Coot: white bill and white forehead shield. Moorhen: red shield and a red bill with a yellow tip, and flicks a white undertail.
Swamphen: much bigger and purple-blue, with long red legs. Moorhen: dark, with a red bill tipped yellow, and swims more.
Little Pied: small, with a short yellow bill. Pied: much bigger, with a longer bill and a yellow-orange patch in front of the eye.
Darter: very long, thin kinked neck and a dagger bill, often swims with only the neck showing. Little Black: shorter neck, hooked bill, green eye.
Caspian: the biggest tern, with a thick blood-red bill. Greater Crested: lemon-yellow bill and a shaggy black crest.
Gull: red bill and legs, rounder head, and scavenges. Tern: yellow bill, black crest, and plunge-dives for fish.
Pied: black above and white below, on sandy beaches. Sooty: all black, on rocky headlands. Both have a red bill.
Beach: much heavier bill, only on quiet beaches and sandbars. Bush: smaller bill and streaky body, in parks, school grounds and woodland.
Curlew: huge, with a very long down-curved bill. Whimbrel: smaller, with a shorter bill kinked near the tip and a striped crown.
Godwit: long bill that curves slightly up. Curlew: bigger, with a much longer bill that curves down.
Black-fronted: black Y across the chest and a red eye-ring, at fresh water. Red-capped: rusty cap and no chest band, on beaches and saltmarsh.
Plover: rusty cap, runs in quick bursts then stops to pick. Stint: grey-brown sandpiper that feeds in busy flocks, probing non-stop.
Peaceful: small and finely barred, with a blue eye-ring. Bar-shouldered: bigger, with a coppery barred nape and a loud "hook-coo".
Crested: grey with a thin spiky crest, and its wings whistle on take-off. Spotted: no crest, and a black collar dotted with white.
Cuckoo-Dove: plain cinnamon with a very long tail, at rainforest edges. Spotted: shorter tail and a white-spotted black collar, in suburbs.
Wompoo: big, with a purple chest and yellow belly, and a deep "wom-poo". Rose-crowned: small, with a pink cap and orange belly.
Frogmouth: broad, wide bill and sits upright like a broken branch. Boobook: a true owl with a small hooked bill; calls "boo-book".
Powerful: about twice the size, with a slow, deep "woo-hoo". Boobook: small brown owl calling "boo-book".
Barn Owl: pale, with a white heart-shaped face, hunts over paddocks and screeches. Boobook: brown with a darker face; calls "boo-book".
Nightjar: slim and long-winged, and roosts flat on the forest floor. Frogmouth: bulky with a wide bill, and roosts upright on branches.
Drongo: forked fish-tail and sallies after insects from a perch. Male Koel: bigger, with a long rounded tail, and calls "coo-ee".
Crow: bigger, with a white eye and heavy bill, and caws. Male Koel: red eye, slimmer, long tail, and calls "coo-ee".
Crow: much bigger, with a white eye and square tail. Drongo: smaller, with a red eye and a forked fish-tail.
Currawong: yellow eye and a white tip to the tail. Crow: white eye and all glossy black.
Fan-tailed: slate-grey with a rufous chest and a yellow eye-ring. Brush: plainer grey-brown; listen for a repeated "fear-ear" rising in pitch.
Needletail: much bigger, dark, with sickle wings, high and fast, and rarely lands. Welcome Swallow: small, rusty face, forked tail, perches on wires.
Fairy Martin: whole head rufous and a white rump. Welcome Swallow: rusty face only, dark rump and a long forked tail.
Fairy: whole head rufous, clean white rump. Tree: dark crown, dull whitish rump, and nests in tree hollows.
Welcome Swallow: rusty face and a long forked tail. Tree Martin: square tail and a dull white rump.
Woodswallow: grey hood over a clean white belly, stockier, with a short square tail. Welcome Swallow: rusty face and throat and a long forked tail.
Black Kite: darker, with a forked tail. Whistling Kite: sandy-brown with a rounded tail and a descending whistle.
Brahminy: rich chestnut with a white head. Whistling: sandy-brown all over, with a rounded tail.
Osprey: smaller, white head with a dark eye stripe, brown back. Sea-Eagle: huge, grey above and white below, soars on upswept wings.
Wedge-tailed: huge, with a diamond-shaped tail. Black Kite: much smaller, with a forked tail.
Kestrel: rufous, and hovers on the spot. Hobby: darker, dark-capped, and chases prey in fast, dashing flight.
Peregrine: bigger and heavier, with a full black hood. Hobby: smaller and slimmer, with a dark cap.
Both hover over grass. Kite: pale grey and white with black shoulders and red eyes. Kestrel: rufous back.
Harrier: slim, with a white rump, and quarters low over reeds. Whistling Kite: no white rump, soars higher, and whistles.
Laughing: brown eye stripe and only a little blue on the wing. Blue-winged: pale eye, no dark eye stripe, lots of blue on the wings; it barks.
Forest: deep blue, with a white spot before the eye and white wing patches in flight. Sacred: turquoise back and buff underparts.
Torresian: bigger, with a bright white collar, mostly in mangroves. Sacred: smaller, turquoise, with buff underparts.
Sulphur-crested: bigger, with a long yellow crest. Little Corella: smaller, short crest and a blue-grey patch around the eye.
Rainbow: blue head and red-orange chest. Scaly-breasted: all green, with yellow scalloping on the chest.
Little: tiny, with a red face and high buzzy calls. Scaly-breasted: bigger, green face, yellow scalloping on the chest.
King-Parrot male: scarlet head and chest, green wings and no blue cheeks. Crimson Rosella: crimson with blue cheeks and blue in the wings.
Yellow-tailed: huge, with a yellow cheek patch and yellow tail panels. Glossy: smaller, red tail panels, and feeds on she-oak cones.
Catbird: chunky and emerald green, with a wailing cat-like call. Satin: males glossy blue-black; females olive-green above with scaly pale underparts.
Variegated males have chestnut shoulder patches. Superb males have none: just electric blue and black.
Red-backed male: jet black with a scarlet back, in long grass. Superb male: electric blue and black.
Spotted: dotted all over with white spots and a red rump. Striated: striped crown and yellow eyebrow; calls "chip-chip".
Scrubwren: pale eye, stays low in dense shrubs and scolds. Brown Gerygone: tiny and plainer, flits higher and twitters "what-is-it".
White-throated: white throat above a yellow belly. Mangrove: plain grey and white, in mangroves.
Red-browed: olive, with a scarlet eyebrow and rump. Double-barred: white owl-like face and two thin black bars across the chest.
Mannikin: chestnut chest with a black band below it. Munia: brown head and a finely scalloped chest.
Cisticola: tiny and buzzy; breeding males have a golden cap. Grassbird: bigger and streaky, with a rufous cap and long tail.
Reed Warbler: plain brown, singing from reedbeds. Grassbird: streaky, with a rufous cap and a long tail.
Myzomela male: whole head and chest scarlet. Mistletoebird male: glossy blue-black above, with a scarlet throat and undertail and a pale belly.
Myna: brown, with a black head and a yellow bill and eye skin. Starling: glossy black, with white spots in winter.
Noisy Miner: a native grey honeyeater with a black crown and yellow eye patch. Common Myna: introduced, brown, with a black head and yellow bill.
Bell Miner: olive-green, with ringing "tink" notes in gullies. Noisy Miner: grey with a black crown, in noisy gangs.
Noisy: bigger, bald black head with a knob on the bill. Little: smaller, with blue-grey face skin and no knob.
Lewin's: dark olive with a yellow crescent ear patch. Yellow-faced: grey-brown with a yellow stripe under the eye, edged in black.
Blue-faced: bigger, olive back and a bright blue face patch. Noisy Miner: grey, with a yellow eye patch and black crown.
Golden male: golden chest, black collar and white throat. Rufous male: grey back, black necklace and a rufous belly.
Oriole: streaky white chest and a red bill. Male Figbird: black head and red skin around the eye. Female Figbirds are streaky too, with a dark bill.
Willie-wagtail: smaller, black throat and white belly, wags its tail side to side. Magpie-lark: bigger, pied wings and a pale eye.
Rufous: glowing orange rump and tail, in rainforest. Grey: grey, with a white eyebrow and white tail edges.
Black-faced: blue-grey with a black face and rufous belly. Spectacled: black mask, orange chest and white tail tips.
Magpie: bigger, all-black front with a white nape. Magpie-lark: smaller and slimmer, white on the face or throat, pale eye, duets "pee-o-wit".
Pied Butcherbird: white chest and belly under a black hood, and a hooked bill. Magpie: black chest and belly.
Pied Butcherbird: black hood with a white collar and a heavy hooked bill. Magpie-lark: pale eye, slim bill and a duetted "pee-o-wit".
Grey: grey back, black cap and white throat. Pied: black hood and throat with a white collar.
Whiptail: pale grey, with a white cheek stripe and a very long tail. Eastern Grey: bigger, plain face without a cheek stripe.
Wallaroo: stocky and shaggy, with a bare black nose, on rocky hills. Eastern Grey: taller and leaner, grazing in mobs on open grass.
Red-necked: grey with a rusty neck and shoulders and a white upper-lip stripe. Swamp: dark and shaggy, with a yellow-orange belly.
Whiptail: pale grey with a white cheek stripe, in groups on open hillsides. Red-necked: rusty neck and shoulders, at forest edges.
Red-necked: reddish neck and shoulders, grazes lawns at dusk. Red-legged: rusty legs and cheeks, shyer, and stays in rainforest.
Pademelon: small and compact, with a short tail, beside rainforest. Wallaby: bigger, with a long tail, at forest edges.
Brushtail: bigger, big pointed ears and a bushy black tail. Ringtail: smaller, with a thin white-tipped tail that curls like a spring.
Short-eared: dark and glossy, with short rounded ears, in wet forest. Common Brushtail: grey, with big pointed ears.
Squirrel: larger, with a fluffier, broader tail, in old woodland. Krefft's: smaller, with a slimmer tail.
Feathertail: mouse-sized, with a flat, feather-like tail. Krefft's: much bigger, with a dark back stripe and a bushy tail.
Grey-headed: grey head with a rusty collar. Black: dark all over the head and body.
Little Red: smaller and reddish-brown, in huge nomadic camps. Grey-headed: bigger, with a grey head and rusty collar.
Long-nosed: grey-brown with a very long, pointed snout, in moist forest. Northern Brown: coarse brown fur and a shorter snout, in leafy suburbs.
Platypus: a duck-like bill; look for rings on still pools at dawn and dusk. Rakali: a rat-like face and a white-tipped tail.
Antechinus: pointed face and orange-yellow feet and rump, busy even by day in winter. Bush Rat: blunter face and rounded ears, and shy.
Dugong: plump with no fin on its back; a broad back and fluke tail break the surface. Dolphin: sleek, with a curved fin on its back.
Free-tailed: big, hunts high over open country, with a loud "tik-tik" people can hear. Gould's Wattled: small, out early at dusk around lights.
Long-necked: neck nearly as long as its shell. Krefft's: shorter neck, with a pale yellow stripe behind the eye.
Saw-shelled: serrated rear edge to the shell and a spiky neck, in clear streams. Krefft's: pale yellow stripe behind the eye, in park lakes.
Loggerhead: very big head and a reddish-brown shell. Green: smaller, rounded head, and grazes seagrass.
Lace Monitor: huge, dark with pale bands, forked tongue, and climbs trees. Water Dragon: crest along the back and a banded tail, beside water.
Bearded: spiky and grey, perches on posts and logs and puffs out a dark beard. Water Dragon: banded tail, beside creeks and in city parks.
Jacky: smaller and slimmer, with a yellow mouth lining. Bearded: chunkier, with a spiky beard it puffs out.
Angle-headed: clings motionless to rainforest trunks, with a spiky crest behind the head. Water Dragon: basks by water and has a banded tail.
Land Mullet: glossy black all over, at rainforest edges. Blue-tongue: banded grey-brown, and flashes a blue tongue.
Land Mullet: glossy black. Major Skink: brown with dark flecks, living in family groups in hollow logs and rock piles.
Water Skink: much bigger and golden-striped, on rocks by creeks. Garden Sunskink: tiny and bronze, in every garden.
Weasel Skink: a white mark behind the eye, in shady, moist spots. Garden Sunskink: bronze, often with a pale side stripe, in sunny gardens.
Burton's: wedge-shaped snout and visible ear holes, and harmless. Eastern Brown: no ear holes and highly venomous. Keep away from any snake.
Common Tree Snake: slender, green, blue or black with a yellow belly, active by day. Brown Tree Snake: banded, with big eyes, hunts at night.
Red-bellied Black: bigger, red-pink belly edge, often by water. Small-eyed: smaller, hides under logs by day. Both venomous: keep away.
Keelback: olive-brown with keeled scales, and not dangerous. Red-bellied Black: glossy black with a red-pink belly edge, and venomous.
Whipsnake: slender and grey, with a pale ring around big eyes. Eastern Brown: plain brown and highly venomous. Keep well away from both.
Carpet Python: thick-bodied, with blotches. Brown Tree Snake: slimmer, banded, with big eyes, and hunts at night.
Green Tree Frog: plump, with a deep "crawk crawk". Graceful: slimmer, with orange thighs, a golden eye, and a long "aaarrk".
Leaf-green: a gold-edged dark stripe through the eye, by rainforest creeks. Graceful: orange thighs and a golden eye, near ponds and gardens.
Dwarf: tiny (2.5 cm) and calls "wreek, pip-pip". Graceful: nearly twice the size, with orange thighs.
Bleating: fawn, with a dark stripe down each side and a piercing bleat. Naked: plain fawn-grey, dark band through the eye, and a grating trill.
Stony Creek: brown, by rocky creeks; breeding males turn lemon-yellow. Leaf-green: slender and green.
Emerald-spotted: grey-brown with tiny emerald flecks and a cross-shaped pupil. Green Tree Frog: plump and green.
Rocket: long legs, pointy nose and a rapid "wick-wick-wick". Striped Marsh: stockier, with a pale mid-back line, and a single "tok".
Salmon-striped: salmon-pink stripes on a brown back. Striped Marsh: dark stripes and a pale mid-back line; calls "tok" from garden ponds.
Spotted Grass: spotted grey-green, with a machine-gun "uk-uk-uk". Striped Marsh: striped, with a single "tok".
Easiest by call. Beeping: a sheep-like "eeeek". Common Eastern: a "crick-crick-crick" chorus. Both are tiny and call mostly in the cooler months.
Wallum: only in acid wallum swamps on the coast, calling a tinkling "tching". Common Eastern: widespread, with a "crick-crick-crick".
Pobblebonk: bigger, with red patches on its sides and a resonant "bonk". Ornate: squat and patterned, with a short "unk".
Great Barred: big, with long barred legs, on rainforest floors; calls a deep "wark". Tusked: warty, with a red-and-black marbled belly.
Blue Triangle: a band of electric-blue triangles. Pale Triangle: rows of pale green triangles.
Macleay's: green with black markings and long tails, in mountain rainforest. Pale Triangle: black with rows of pale green triangles.
Birdwing: huge, black and green, in lowland rainforest. Orchard: black and white; females have red and blue spots.
Chequered: tailless, with a chequered black-and-cream pattern. Orchard: big black-and-white swallowtail of citrus gardens.
Caper White: white with heavy black edges. Lemon Migrant: plain pale lemon or white, and very fast.
Grass Yellow: small, lemon-yellow with black wing edges, low over lawns. Lemon Migrant: bigger and faster, plain pale lemon or white.
Scarlet Jezebel: a bright scarlet band across the underwing. Black Jezebel: red and yellow spots underneath rather than a band.
Blue Tiger: pale blue streaks and spots on black. Common Crow: dark brown with white spots around the edges.
Meadow Argus: brown, with big blue-and-orange eyespots. Painted Lady: orange and black, with small blue-centred eyespots on the hindwings.
Evening Brown: leaf-brown, flies at dusk and rests in leaf litter by day. Dingy Bush-brown: plain brown, flits low along forest edges by day.
Pea-blue: tiny tails and eyespots, around flowering peas. Grass-blue: tiny lilac-blue, flutters just above lawns.
Lesser Wanderer: orange, with black veins and white spots on the wingtips. Rustic: orange-brown with a dark wingtip, gliding at rainforest edges.
Spotted Gum: smooth bark dimpled in patches of grey, cream and pink. Scribbly Gum: smooth white bark covered in squiggly scribbles.
Forest Red Gum: smooth blotched bark and long horn-shaped buds. Spotted Gum: dimpled patches of grey, cream and pink.
Ironbark: hard, deeply furrowed dark bark. Bloodwood: rough, flaky bark that oozes red sap.
Tallowwood: soft, fibrous orange-brown bark. Ironbark: hard, deeply furrowed dark grey bark.
Brush Box: smooth salmon-pink upper bark over a rough lower trunk. Spotted Gum: smooth all the way down, in dimpled patches.
Paperbark: layered, papery white bark and creamy bottlebrush flowers. Swamp Mahogany: spongy red-brown bark.
Bottlebrush: red flowers on drooping branches. Paperbark: creamy flowers and layered, papery white bark.
Coastal: pale yellow flower spikes and leaves silvery underneath. Wallum: thick, serrated leaves and fat greenish-yellow cones.
Brisbane Wattle: pale yellow ball flowers. Early Black Wattle: golden flower spikes.
Hoop: tufted branches and bark that peels in hoops. Bunya: dome-shaped crown, sharp leaves and huge cones.
Cabbage Tree: round fan leaves, deeply divided. Piccabeen: feathery fronds, lilac flowers and red fruit.
Flame Tree: scarlet bell flowers on bare branches in early summer. Firewheel: red-and-orange flowers arranged like the spokes of a wheel.
Tell them by where they grow. Coastal: on dunes and in the sea breeze. Swamp: on estuaries and tidal flats.
Purple Coral Pea: purple pea flowers in late winter. Dusky Coral Pea: a stronger climber with larger, dark-red flowers.
Elkhorn: a shield of brown leaves with forked fronds. Bird's Nest: glossy, undivided fronds in a nest-shaped rosette.
Pink Rock: small, with sprays of pink-mauve flowers. King: large, with long sprays of cream-yellow flowers.
Little: short throat feathers and a quick, repeated "ark-ark-ark". Australian: long shaggy throat feathers and a slower call with a trailing wail.
Brown: rusty forehead, red eye and streaks mainly on the throat and chest. Striated: pale streaks over the crown and cheeks, with streaking extending onto the belly.
Buff-rumped: buff rump, plain brown crown and a pale eye. Yellow-rumped: bright yellow rump, black crown dotted white and a bold pale eyebrow.
Yellow: fine pointed bill, yellow underparts and pale streaks on the cheek. Weebill: short stubby bill, pale eye and plainer face.
Brown: smaller, with a rusty forehead, red eye and finely streaked chest. Scrubwren: bold white eyebrow over a dark face, with a pale eye.
Brown: red eye, rusty forehead and dark streaks on the throat. Buff-rumped: pale eye, plain throat and a buff rump above a dark tail band.
Striated: pale-streaked rusty crown and dark streaks down the underparts. Yellow: plain olive crown, yellow underparts and pale streaks mainly on the cheek.
Striated: streaked crown and underparts, usually feeding in treetops. Buff-rumped: plain crown and chest, pale eye and buff rump, often feeding near the ground.
Red: red cheek wattles and a yellow belly, with a larger body. Little: no wattles or yellow belly, with finer white streaks underneath.
Eastern: white cheeks and a yellow belly below the red chest. Crimson: blue cheeks, even on green juveniles, with adults mostly crimson below.

Hoary-headed: white head streaks when breeding, otherwise a dark cap above pale cheeks. Australasian: chestnut neck and yellow face spot when breeding, otherwise a darker cheek with the cap extending below the eye.
Great: much bigger, with a heavy bill, yellow throat skin and a white cheek patch. Little Black: slim bill and dark face, with no white cheek patch.
Black-faced: black skin around the eye and bill, with a dark bill. Pied: yellow-orange skin in front of the eye and a paler, heavier bill.
Pacific: huge, with a deep heavy bill, black back as an adult and brown plumage when young. Silver: much smaller, with a slim bill and pale grey back; young birds have mottled wings.
Long-billed: long pointed upper bill and a red band across the throat. Little: short bill and no red throat band, though the face can look pink.
Musk: green chest and face with red forehead and ear patches. Rainbow: blue head and red-orange chest, with a larger body.
Musk: red forehead and ear patches, blue crown and green chest. Purple-crowned: smaller, with an orange forehead, purple crown and pale blue chest.
Grey: grey to sooty plumage and no white at the tail base, with ringing clinking calls. Pied: black with white at both the base and tip of the tail, calling "curra-wong".
Falcon: two dark face stripes and pointed wings, with a shorter tail. Goshawk: rounded wings, long barred tail and a strong brow over the eye.
Falcon: bigger and heavier, with two dark face stripes and broad wings. Kestrel: smaller and slimmer, with a rusty back, narrow pointed wings and one dark cheek stripe.
Eagle: broad wings with pale panels against dark flight feathers, a shorter tail and feathered legs. Kite: longer rounded tail and pale underwings crossed by dark bands, with bare lower legs.
Sparrowhawk: thin legs, long middle toe and usually a square or notched tail tip. Goshawk: thick legs, heavy brow and a more rounded tail tip.
Sharp-tailed: rusty cap, pale eyebrow, yellowish legs and a short, slightly curved bill. Curlew: black legs and a longer down-curved bill, with a white rump in flight.
Curlew: taller, with longer legs and a long down-curved bill. Stint: tiny and short-legged, with a short, almost straight bill.
Knot: stockier, with a straight bill, greenish legs and a finely barred pale rump. Curlew: slimmer, with a down-curved bill, black legs and a clean white rump.
Greenshank: bigger and heavier, with a sturdy bill that curves slightly up. Marsh: slimmer, with very long thin legs and a fine straight bill.

Fairy: white between the eye and bill, with an orange-yellow bill usually lacking a black tip when breeding. Little: black line from eye to bill and a black-tipped yellow bill when breeding; winter birds are harder.

Whiskered: stouter bill and grey rump, with white cheeks above a dark grey belly when breeding. White-winged: finer bill and white rump, with a black body and white upperwings when breeding, or a dark ear spot in winter.
Banded: white head and neck, with a chestnut breast band in adults. Pied: black hindneck and no chestnut breast band; young Banded have a plain white head and neck.

Blue-billed: compact, with a broad bill, bright blue on breeding males, and finely barred brown females. Musk: larger, with a dark wedge-shaped bill and bulky head; adult males have a hanging throat lobe.
Shoveler: broad spoon-shaped bill, even on mottled brown females. Pacific Black: narrower bill and bold dark stripes across a pale face.

Mallard: females have a softer face pattern and orange-and-dark bill, males a green head and curled tail feathers. Pacific Black: bold face stripes and a grey bill; hybrids mix these marks and can be hard to identify.
Australian: bigger, with a red base to its green bill and white flecks on an olive-brown back. Baillon's: tiny, with a plain green bill and a brown back marked with jagged white streaks.
Spotless: dark slate underparts, plain brown back and red legs. Baillon's: paler grey below, with white markings on the back, barred flanks and dull greenish legs.
Spotless: all dark slate below, an unmarked brown back and red legs. Australian: grey face and breast, a white-flecked back, a red base to the bill and greenish legs.
Nativehen: upright black tail, green bill and bright pink-red legs. Moorhen: red bill tipped yellow, white flank stripe and white edges to the undertail.
Lewin's: long pinkish bill, rusty crown and grey chest, without a bold white eyebrow. Buff-banded: bold white eyebrow, chestnut eye stripe and a buff band across the barred breast.
Skylark: small crest, stocky body and a shorter tail, often singing high overhead. Pipit: slimmer, with a bold pale eyebrow and longer tail that it pumps while walking.
Blackbird: females are plain brown above, with mottling mainly on the throat and chest and a longer tail. Bassian: bold dark scallops across both the back and pale underparts, with a stockier body.
Song: plain brown back and separate dark arrowhead spots on a cream breast. Bassian: dark scallops across the back and underparts, with a larger, stockier body.
White-naped: black cap and red skin above the eye, with a white nape band. Brown-headed: brown head and creamy yellow eye skin, with a pale nape band.
New Holland: white adult eye and bold black-and-white streaking across the chest. Crescent: dark eye and black crescents down the sides of a mostly white breast.
White-plumed: yellowish face and a narrow white neck plume edged black. Singing: broad black eye stripe with yellow below it, and no white neck plume.

Flame: males have a grey back and orange-red reaching up the throat, females a plain brown breast. Scarlet: males have a black throat and large white forehead patch, females usually a reddish breast wash.

Scarlet: males have a black head, large white forehead patch and scarlet breast, females a warm reddish breast wash. Rose: males have a grey head, tiny white forehead spot and rose-pink breast, females usually a plainer grey-brown breast.

Rose: males have a grey back, pink breast and white lower belly, with white outer tail feathers in both sexes. Pink: males have a sooty back and pink belly, while brown females have buff wing bars; both sexes lack white tail edges.
Tree: chestnut cap and a black spot on each white cheek in both sexes. House: males have a grey crown and unspotted cheeks, females a plain brown head with a pale eyebrow.
Dusky: smoky brown below, with a thin white leading edge to the wing and white tail tips. White-breasted: clean white belly below a grey hood, with a white rump.
White-throated: clear white throat and streaked flanks, with a small orange cheek spot on females. Red-browed: rusty eyebrow, grey throat and fine streaks across the underparts.
Grassbird: streaked crown and chest, with a rounded tail and thin mournful whistles. Reed Warbler: plain brown back and pale chest, with a longer bill and loud chattering song.
Fieldwren: bold pale eyebrow and a cocked tail with white tips, often singing from low bushes. Grassbird: fainter eyebrow and plain brown tail, usually held low as it slips through reeds.
Pallid: bigger, with pale grey underparts and a dark eye stripe, calling repeated rising whistles. Fan-tailed: smaller, with a rufous chest and yellow eye-ring, calling a descending trill.
Horsfield's: bold pale eyebrow, dark eye stripe and broken bars down the chest. Shining: greener back, plainer face and more complete bars across the underparts.
Olive: grey head over a whitish, finely barred throat, with an olive-brown back and buff underparts. Golden: females have a paler grey throat and breast, with yellowish under the tail.

Satin: males have glossy blue-black backs and a breast boundary curving down at the sides, females a bluish crown sheen. Leaden: males have greyer backs and a boundary curving up at the sides, females a plain grey crown; young birds are harder.
Swift: long pointed maroon tail, red face and throat, and red wing edges. Musk: shorter green tail, green throat and separate red forehead and ear patches.
Blue-winged: small, with a blue forehead band and broad blue wing patch. Red-rumped: larger, with a longer tail and no blue forehead band; males have a red rump, females are dull olive.
Brush: chestnut shoulders and a dark grey breast, with a chestnut forehead on males. Common: larger, with a pinkish breast, bold white cheek stripe and pale forehead on males.

Hooded: larger, with a black hood, white collar and red eye-ring as an adult. Red-capped: smaller, with a rusty cap and pale face; young Hooded have a dark bill and a pale collar behind a grey-brown head.
Red-kneed: black cap and broad breast band, white throat and red upper legs. Black-fronted: white forehead, black eye stripe and a narrower black Y across the chest.
Stubble: bold pale back stripes and a white belly, with a black breast patch on males. Brown: warmer brown below, with fine pale streaks and dark barring, and no black breast patch.
Chough: red adult eye, slender down-curved bill and broad white wing patches in flight. Raven: white adult eye, heavier bill and all-black wings; young birds of both have dark eyes.
Freckled: peaked head, slightly upturned bill and fine cream speckles over dark plumage. Pacific Black: flatter crown and bold dark stripes across a pale face.
